introduction: This level drives into structural configurations and structural/stereo-isomerism. It also introduces the structural predictions of Valence Bond Theory (VBT), explaining how d-orbital electron distribution determines hybridization, 3D molecular geometry, and the magnetic properties of complexes.

core_concepts.title: Structural Isomerism
core_concepts.description:
Compounds with identical molecular formulas but different connectivity of atoms:
1. Ionization Isomerism: Yields different ions in solution due to exchange of counter ions and inner ligands (e.g., $[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Br$ gives $Br^-$, while $[Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4$ gives $SO_4^{2-}$).
2. Linkage Isomerism: Arises when ambidentate ligands bind via different donor atoms (e.g., $[Co(NH_3)_5(ONO)]^{2+}$ vs. $[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]^{2+}$).
3. Coordination Isomerism: Occurs in salts featuring both complex cation and complex anion species via interchange of ligands between the two centers (e.g., $[Cr(NH_3)_6][Co(CN)_6]$ and $[Co(NH_3)_6][Cr(CN)_6]$).
4. Solvate/Hydrate Isomerism: Differs by whether water molecules are bound directly inside the sphere as ligands or outside as water of crystallization (e.g., $[Cr(H_2O)_6]Cl_3$ [violet] vs. $[Cr(H_2O)_5Cl]Cl_2 \cdot H_2O$ [green]).

core_concepts.title: Stereoisomerism: Geometrical Isomerism (GI)
core_concepts.description:
Occurs due to different spatial arrangements of ligands around the central metal.
- Square Planar ($CN=4$): Compounds of type $MA_2B_2$ exhibit **cis** (identical ligands adjacent, $90^\circ$) and **trans** (identical ligands opposite, $180^\circ$) forms. Tetrahedral complexes never show GI due to perfectly equidistant relative spots ($109.5^\circ$).
- Octahedral ($CN=6$): $MA_4B_2$ shows cis/trans forms. Complexes of type $MA_3B_3$ (e.g., $[Co(NH_3)_3(NO_2)_3]$) show unique **facial (fac)** and **meridional (mer)** isomers.

core_concepts.title: Stereoisomerism: Optical Isomerism (OI)
core_concepts.description:
Chiral complexes that lack a plane of symmetry form non-superimposable mirror images called enantiomers (dextro and laevo forms). Crucial rules for exams:
1. Cis-isomers of chelated octahedral complexes like $\text{cis-}[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^+$ lack a plane of symmetry and are ALWAYS optically active.
2. Trans-isomers of the exact same complexes possess a perfect internal mirror plane and are ALWAYS optically inactive (meso-like behavior).

core_concepts.title: Valence Bond Theory (VBT) Framework
core_concepts.description:
VBT links hybridization with magnetic profiles based on orbital overlapping. Under the influence of ligands, the $(n-1)d, ns, np,$ or $nd$ orbitals hybridize.
- $CN=4$: Can hybridize to $sp^3$ (Tetrahedral geometry) or $dsp^2$ (Square Planar geometry).
- $CN=6$: Can hybridize to $d^2sp^3$ (Inner Orbital Octahedral Complex, using lower $(n-1)d$ orbitals) or $sp^3d^2$ (Outer Orbital Octahedral Complex, using outer $nd$ orbitals).

important_entities.name: The $fac$ and $mer$ Isomer Split
important_entities.key_fact: Applies exclusively to octahedral complexes of type $MA_3B_3$.
important_entities.significance: In the facial ($fac$) isomer, three identical ligands occupy the three corners of the same octahedral face. In the meridional ($mer$) isomer, the three identical ligands map out an arc around the meridian of the octahedron. They display distinctly unique electronic dipole moments and spectral signatures.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Students assume that because organic carbon needs four different groups to be asymmetric, any tetrahedral metal complex with four different ligands ($MABCD$) must be optically active. While theoretically true, in inorganic chemistry, unsymmetrical tetrahedral complexes are chemically extremely labile—they invert configuration rapidly at room temperature. Thus, they cannot be resolved into stable optical isomers. Look strictly for octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands for stable optical activity!

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Strong pairs them up, Weak leaves them alone
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: When predicting hybridization via VBT: Strong field ligands (like $CN^-, CO, en, NH_3$) force the unpaired d-electrons of the metal to pair up against Hund's rule, clearing out inner d-orbitals to form inner orbital complexes ($d^2sp^3$). Weak field ligands (like $F^-, Cl^-, OH^-, H_2O$) cannot force pairing, resulting in high-spin outer orbital complexes ($sp^3d^2$).

exam_strategy_tips:
To solve complex VBT problems quickly (e.g., predicting the properties of $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ vs. $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$):
1. Identify the metal oxidation state ($Ni^{2+} \rightarrow 3d^8$).
2. Look at the ligand: $CN^-$ is strong, forces pairing of the two unpaired electrons in $3d$, leaving one $3d$ orbital vacant $\rightarrow dsp^2$ (Square Planar, Diamagnetic). $Cl^-$ is weak, no pairing occurs $\rightarrow sp^3$ (Tetrahedral, Paramagnetic with 2 unpaired electrons).
